extra_misconceptions.fact: Requirement 1 explicitly mandates choosing a different racial, ethnic, or religious group for each of the two selected options.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Both activities in Requirement 1 can focus on the same cultural group if you visit two separate locations.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Scouts must attend a live cultural event, visit a physical institution or museum, or interact directly with community members.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Watching a television documentary at home satisfies the museum exhibit or festival attendance options in Requirement 1.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Many religious services strictly prohibit photography during rituals, so you must ask a host leader for permission beforehand.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Taking photographs inside a house of worship is always acceptable as long as the camera flash is turned off.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Option 1d requires you to both learn the traditional song, dance, poem, or story and actively teach it to a group of friends.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Learning a traditional song or story for Option 1d is complete as soon as you can perform it for your counselor.

extra_socratic_questions: What rule governs how many distinct cultural groups you must select across the two field activities in Requirement 1?
Which details separate an objective field observation from a personal assumption when visiting a house of worship?
What specific provenance details should you record in your field notebook when documenting a cultural exhibit or artifact?
Why must a Scout verify dress code and photography rules with the host before entering a religious institution?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Even isolated societies evolve in response to local climate, geography, generational shifts, and internal inventions.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An isolated society with zero outside contact experiences no internal cultural change or technological innovation over time.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Coexisting groups exchange language, cuisine, music, and civic traditions multidirectionally across all community segments.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cultural diffusion only moves in one direction, from the largest majority population to smaller minority communities.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pluralistic cities often preserve distinct neighborhood traditions while building shared civic institutions and public norms.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Three distinct groups sharing one city will inevitably erase their heritage and merge into a single uniform culture.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Without external trade routes, an isolated group relies entirely on local ecosystems for building materials, crops, and tools.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Geographic isolation affects only a society's language and has no impact on its diet, housing styles, or trade economy.

extra_socratic_questions: What changes occur in a city's foodways, architecture, and civic calendar when three isolated groups begin sharing it?
What distinguishes mutual cultural diffusion from forced assimilation when three distinct groups share one municipality?
Which observable neighborhood markers indicate that multiple cultural groups actively shape a shared urban landscape?
Why does preparing side-by-side comparison notes across all three groups prevent stereotyping during your simulation?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Ethnic groups encompass diverse religious beliefs, regional practices, and varying levels of observance among families.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every member of a specific ethnic group practices the exact same religion and observes identical holiday traditions.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Religious customs stem from sacred beliefs and texts, whereas social customs include secular etiquette, dress, and folkways.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Social customs and religious laws are identical concepts because both guide how people behave in public settings.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Diverse cultures frequently share core values such as honoring elders, welcoming guests, and celebrating major life milestones.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Groups with different languages and religions share no common social values regarding family or community hospitality.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Requirement 3 requires analyzing both the differences and the similarities across all three of your selected cultural groups.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Comparing two of your chosen groups is sufficient if the third group has a very different historical background.

extra_socratic_questions: What categories of daily life help you compare both religious and social customs systematically across all three groups?
What criterion separates a sacred religious obligation from a secular social custom practiced within the same community?
Which shared life-cycle milestones reveal common core values across three otherwise distinct cultural traditions?
Why should you verify custom descriptions against reputable community sources before presenting your comparison matrix?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Each of the three individuals you discuss must represent a different racial, ethnic, or religious background in America.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: All three historical figures chosen for Requirement 4 may come from the same racial, ethnic, or religious background.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Scientists, inventors, artists, labor organizers, educators, and religious leaders have all shaped American life and progress.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Only presidents, military generals, or elected politicians qualify as having made a major contribution to our country.

extra_misconceptions.fact: You must explain the specific contribution each person made and how their work benefited or transformed the United States.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Reciting a person's birth and death dates fulfills the requirement without explaining the impact of their achievement.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Immigrants from around the world have made foundational contributions to American science, industry, culture, and governance.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A person must have been born inside the United States to be credited with a meaningful contribution to our country.

extra_socratic_questions: What selection rule ensures that the three historical figures you profile satisfy the diversity condition in Requirement 4?
What evidence distinguishes a lasting contribution to the United States from short-term celebrity or personal wealth?
Which primary or archival sources best verify how an individual's work changed American law, science, arts, or civic life?
Why does understanding the social barriers a figure faced clarify the historical significance of their contribution?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Requirement 5 specifies delivering your talk and leading a discussion before your Scout unit or a class at school.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Giving a private talk only to your merit badge counselor satisfies the presentation requirement in Requirement 5.

extra_misconceptions.fact: After giving your talk on intergroup relations, you must actively lead a group discussion on improving mutual understanding.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Reading a prepared speech and sitting down immediately completes all parts of the Requirement 5 presentation.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An honest talk examines both how diverse groups cooperated and how communities overcame prejudice, tension, and injustice.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Historical accounts of intergroup relations in America should only mention peaceful cooperation and ignore past conflicts.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Effective facilitators use open questions and courteous listening to help participants explore practical ways to build respect.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leading a productive discussion requires the speaker to debate and defeat every audience member who shares a question.

extra_socratic_questions: What two distinct communication roles must you fulfill before your Scout unit or school class to complete Requirement 5?
What facilitation skill separates leading an interactive group discussion from delivering a one-way speech to your unit?
Which open-ended prompt types encourage patrol members to propose concrete ways groups can build mutual understanding?
Why should a presenter establish ground rules based on the Scout Law before opening the floor to sensitive topics?
